title: The Wright Brothers Argue Their Way to Flight
text:
Wilbur and Orville Wright never married. They lived together in their father's house in Dayton, Ohio, ran a bicycle shop together, and from 1899 worked together on the problem of flight. Their father, Milton, a bishop of the United Brethren Church, had brought home a toy helicopter when they were boys, and their sister Katharine kept the household going and later managed much of their correspondence.

The brothers were famous among their few employees for their arguments. Charlie Taylor, their mechanic, remembered them shouting at each other in the shop. Yet the arguments were a method. One would take a position, the other would attack it, and sometimes they would switch sides. When their glider of 1901 performed badly, they built a wind tunnel and tested some two hundred wing shapes, and discovered that the published lift tables everyone relied on were wrong.

On 17 December 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville made the first powered, controlled flight, lasting twelve seconds. Wilbur had won the coin toss three days earlier but stalled on takeoff. That day they flew four times, taking turns. Wilbur said later that they had lived together, played together, worked together and thought together. They shared credit and held their patents jointly.
lesson: Close partners do not need to agree to work well together. Honest argument between people who trust each other can find what polite agreement misses.
people: Wilbur Wright, Orville Wright, Milton Wright, Katharine Wright
location: Dayton, Ohio and Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, USA
source: The Papers of Wilbur and Orville Wright, ed. Marvin W. McFarland (1953); David McCullough, The Wright Brothers (2015)
place: Wright Brothers National Memorial, Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, USA
